sections.heading: What you're seeing
sections.body: High-level usage stats for the selected period: sessions, prompts, tokens, cache efficiency, and estimated API cost.

sections.heading: Daily / Hourly Token Usage
sections.body: Stacked bar chart showing output tokens, non-cached input, cache reads, and cache creation over time. When period is "Day", shows hourly breakdown.

sections.heading: Token Breakdown
sections.body: Doughnut chart of total token distribution across the four categories: output, input, cache read, and cache creation.

sections.heading: Cache Usage
sections.body: Shows how effectively prompt caching is working. Higher cache read % means less redundant token processing and lower cost.

sections.heading: Cumulative API Value vs Plan Fee
sections.body: Tracks how much API value you've consumed over time against your monthly plan fee. If the line exceeds the dashed plan fee line, you're getting more than 1× value from your subscription.

sections.heading: What this tab shows
sections.body: Where your money goes: cost by model, the most expensive tools and MCP servers, your priciest sessions and prompts, and what each successful task actually costs.

sections.heading: Cost per Successful Task
sections.body: The headline figure is the total spent on all task attempts divided by the number that succeeded — i.e. what you really pay for each task that works, including the cost of the attempts that failed along the way. It decomposes as mean cost per attempt ÷ success rate, so either cheaper attempts or a higher success rate lowers it.

sections.heading: How outcomes are decided
sections.body: Each task is auto-classified as success, failed, in-flight, or unobservable from git activity and signal confidence. You can override any task with the ✓ (success), ~ (partial), or ✗ (fail) buttons, or ⌫ to clear your label. Manual labels always take priority over the proxy.

sections.heading: Coverage and how much to trust it
sections.body: The rate is computed only over "observable" tasks — those with enough signal to judge. The coverage badge shows how many of your total tasks that is. When coverage is below 20% a warning appears: the number rests on a small slice and should be read as a rough guide rather than an exact figure.

sections.heading: Per-model table
sections.body: Cost per successful task, success rate, and observable count broken out by model, so you can see which model gives you the most reliable result per dollar.

sections.heading: What this tab is for
sections.body: Assign each project to the subscription that should be billed for it. Projects are ranked by cost, so classifying the top few covers most of your spend.

sections.heading: VS Code only
sections.body: Project classification is available in the VS Code panel; the browser-served dashboard does not offer it.

sections.heading: Top Projects
sections.body: Horizontal bar chart of your most token-intensive projects. Useful for understanding where your usage is concentrated.

sections.heading: Token Share by Project
sections.body: Pie chart showing what percentage of total tokens each project consumes. Quickly identifies which projects dominate your usage.

sections.heading: Energy Usage by Project
sections.body: Pie chart of estimated energy consumption per project. Only shown when energy data is available.

sections.heading: Thinking Intensity by Project
sections.body: Measures extended thinking blocks per prompt for each project. Higher values indicate projects requiring deeper reasoning — complex debugging, architectural decisions, or nuanced code generation. Low values suggest straightforward tasks. A sudden increase may signal growing codebase complexity.

sections.heading: Nature of Work by Project
sections.body: Shows how Claude's effort breaks down across five categories for each project: Exploring (reading and searching code), Editing (writing and modifying files), Running (shell commands and builds), Researching (web searches), and Planning (plans and tasks). Reveals whether a project is mostly exploration, active development, or debugging.

sections.heading: 5-Hour Usage Windows
sections.body: Claude tracks usage in rolling 5-hour windows. Each bar shows the API value consumed in that window. Red bars indicate windows where throttling occurred.

sections.heading: Top Conversations by API Cost
sections.body: Your most expensive individual conversations. Hover for details including prompt count, dominant model, and percentage of plan fee.

sections.heading: Sessions by Entrypoint
sections.body: Pie chart showing how sessions are distributed across entrypoints (CLI, VS Code extension, API, etc.).

sections.heading: What this tab measures
sections.body: Compares the API-equivalent value of your Claude usage against your subscription plan cost. Helps answer: “Should I upgrade or downgrade?”

sections.heading: Plan Verdict
sections.body: “Good Value” means your API-equivalent usage exceeds your plan fee (you’re getting more than you pay). “Underusing” means you’re paying more than the equivalent API cost.

sections.heading: Suggested Plan
sections.body: Based on your average weekly API-equivalent cost, extrapolated to monthly. Compares against Pro ($20), Team Standard ($25), Max 5x ($100), Team Premium ($125), and Max 20x ($200) tiers.

sections.heading: Weekly Activity
sections.body: Bar chart showing sessions and prompts per week. Helps you see your usage patterns and whether your activity level justifies your current plan.

sections.heading: API Cost per 5-Hour Window
sections.body: Shows absolute API-equivalent cost per 5-hour window. Bars are orange for windows that contained an assistant response cut off at the output-token limit (a "truncated output"). Note: Anthropic's 5-hour rate-limit rejections never reach the session logs, so we cannot reliably show a real "% of limit" value.

sections.heading: Windows Per Week
sections.body: Stacked bar showing total 5-hour usage windows per week. The orange segment counts windows that contained a truncated-output response — a non-critical signal that usually points at a single long response being cut off at the output-token limit.

sections.heading: Multi-Account Support
sections.body: If you use multiple Claude accounts (e.g. work team + personal), each account is detected separately with its own plan verdict and cost breakdown.

sections.heading: What this tab measures
sections.body: Analyzes your context management habits: conversation length, context window growth, compaction usage, and cache efficiency. Helps you answer: "Am I managing my context optimally?"

sections.heading: Conversation Length Distribution
sections.body: Histogram of how many prompts your sessions contain. Very long sessions (15+ prompts) without compaction can lead to higher costs and slower responses as the context window fills up.

sections.heading: Context Growth Curve
sections.body: Shows how input tokens grow with each successive prompt in a conversation. A steep curve means context is accumulating fast — consider using /compact or starting new conversations for unrelated tasks.

sections.heading: Cache Efficiency by Length
sections.body: Compares cache hit rates across short vs long conversations. If cache efficiency drops in longer sessions, it may indicate the context is being rebuilt too often or /compact is discarding useful cached context.

sections.heading: Compaction Events
sections.body: Detected instances where input tokens dropped significantly between messages (>40% reduction), indicating /compact was used. Shows the before/after token counts to visualize how much context was reclaimed.

sections.heading: Long Sessions Table
sections.body: Sessions with 15+ prompts, sorted by peak input tokens. The “Compacted?” column shows whether compaction was detected. Sessions marked “No” may have benefited from running /compact to reduce context size and cost.

sections.heading: What this tab measures
sections.body: Analyzes whether you're sending prompts to a more expensive model than necessary. Each user prompt ("turn") is scored for complexity, then classified into a recommended tier: Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus.

sections.heading: Potential Savings
sections.body: Dollar amount you could save if every turn had been routed to the cheapest model capable of handling it. Only counts cases where you used a more expensive model than the classified tier.

sections.heading: Overuse Rate
sections.body: Percentage of classified turns where the actual model was more expensive than the recommended tier. A high overuse rate suggests opportunities to use cheaper models for simple tasks.

sections.heading: Model Usage by Complexity Tier
sections.body: Stacked bar per model, colored by classified tier (green=Haiku, blue=Sonnet, red=Opus). If Opus has a large green or blue segment, those turns could have used a cheaper model.

sections.heading: Opus Complexity Score Distribution
sections.body:
Histogram of complexity scores (0–100) for turns that were sent to Opus. Scores are computed from four signals:

• Output tokens (0–25 pts) — longer responses indicate harder tasks
• Thinking blocks (0–30 pts) — extended thinking is the strongest complexity signal
• Tool complexity (0–25 pts) — Agent, Write, NotebookEdit score highest
• Prompt text analysis (0–20 pts) — keywords like "refactor" or "architect" add points; "fix typo" or "rename" subtract

Bars are colored by tier: green (0–20, Haiku-level), blue (20–40, Sonnet-level), red (40+, Opus-level). Green and blue bars represent Opus turns that may not have needed Opus.

sections.heading: Top Overuse
sections.body: The specific turns with the highest potential savings — cases where an expensive model was used for a task classified as simpler. Shows a preview of the prompt text and the dollar savings if the tier-appropriate model had been used.

sections.heading: What this tab measures
sections.body: Estimates the electricity and CO₂ footprint of your Claude usage. Computed per-message using model-class energy coefficients (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus) and your detected or locale-inferred grid region. Uncertainty is ±55% — Anthropic does not publish per-request energy data.

sections.heading: Grid Region
sections.body: Energy-to-CO₂ conversion uses the carbon intensity of the detected inference region (from inference_geo on each message). Falls back to your locale if no geo is detected. You can see coverage % and which regions were seen.

sections.heading: Cache Savings
sections.body: Cache read tokens are ~3% the energy cost of re-computing them as input tokens. This section shows estimated energy and CO₂ saved by prompt caching.

sections.heading: Environmental Context
sections.body: Converts total energy and CO₂ to tangible units sitting side-by-side in one strip: cubic meters of natural gas a modern combined-cycle gas turbine (~55 % efficiency, LHV ≈ 9.94 kWh/m³) would burn to deliver the same electrical energy (~0.183 m³/kWh), area of solar panels that would take the selected period to generate the same energy in the detected grid region (~20% efficiency × 0.75 performance ratio, scaled down from annual yield), wind-turbine rotations (~1.17 kWh per rotation on a 3 MW onshore turbine at 35% capacity factor), liters of water through a hydroelectric turbine (~4,077 L/kWh at a representative 100 m head with 90% efficiency, via E = m·g·h·η), engineered nuclear-repository volume (canisters + buffer + tunnel excavation, weighted across HLW+ILW+LLW, ~4 mL/kWh), and km travelled by local transit (30 gCO₂/pkm — bus/metro/tram blend) and long-distance electrified train (6 gCO₂/pkm). A journey anchor below the strip snaps the period's driven-km equivalent to a recognizable trip.

sections.heading: How this is calculated
sections.body: A collapsible panel below the equivalents strip shows the full derivation using your period's actual numbers: per-model-class token counts, per-class energy rates (Wh per 1K input/output tokens), PUE overhead, grid intensity, and the arithmetic behind every equivalent. You can audit or reproduce each figure from the tokens the API returned.

sections.heading: Data Sources
sections.body: Lists the upstream citations behind each coefficient: Google's 2025 Gemini inference whitepaper and Epoch AI 2024 for model energy rates; Uptime Institute for PUE; EPA eGRID / EEA / IEA for grid intensity; PVGIS/NREL/World Bank GSA for solar yield; IRENA/IEA for the wind turbine; Posiva KBS-3 / SKB / IAEA for nuclear disposal; UIC and EEA for transport emissions.

sections.heading: Daily and Per-Model Charts
sections.body: Two charts below the equivalents strip: daily energy and CO₂ over the period (left) and total energy by model (right). Both report energy in kWh.

sections.heading: What you can configure
sections.body: Plan type (Pro, Max, Team, Custom) and monthly fee. These are used for plan utilization calculations on the Plan tab. If not set, the tool auto-detects from telemetry.

sections.heading: Cost Alert Thresholds
sections.body: Set daily, weekly, and monthly cost thresholds. When estimated API cost exceeds a threshold, alerts are shown after collection.

sections.heading: Where settings are stored
sections.body: All settings are saved to ~/.claude-stats/config.json. You can also edit this file directly.

sections.heading: What you're seeing
sections.body: The five business questions this tool exists to answer: what AI cost, what it bought, whether it was efficient, whether the setup is right, and what should change. One sentence and one number each, with a link to the evidence behind it.

sections.heading: Cards that say they cannot answer
sections.body: A card with no data states what is missing and how to enable it, instead of showing an empty widget or a fabricated zero. On a fresh install most cards start that way, and each one names the next step.

sections.heading: The alerts strip
sections.body: Shown only when something genuinely needs attention, and deliberately quiet: an alert that fires on noise trains you to ignore the strip.

sections.heading: Cost per ticket
sections.body: Cost attributed to work-item keys (PROJ-123), found in git branch names, commit subjects and prompt text. No ticket system is contacted — the key itself is the entire interface. Rows are cost-descending; expand one to see the sessions behind it and which signal matched.

sections.heading: Coverage
sections.body: What fraction of the period's spend is attributed to any ticket at all. This is normally well below 100%, because work without a key in its branch, commits or prompts cannot be attributed. Read the table as a view of the attributed part, never as the whole bill.

sections.heading: Confidence tiers
sections.body: High means a branch name matched while a project-key allowlist was configured. Medium means a commit subject matched, or a branch matched with no allowlist to filter noise. Low means only prompt text mentioned the key. Two independent signals agreeing upgrade the tier by one step.

sections.heading: Ticket attribution
sections.body: Link the current session to a key, or negate an automatic link that is wrong. A negated link cannot be resurrected by re-extraction. Buttons act only in the VS Code panel — the served page renders them inert, since a LAN visitor must not be able to write to your database.

loading.title: Loading your stats…
loading.subtitle: Crunching your Claude Code history. This can take a few seconds the first time.

noClaudeCode.title: Welcome to Claude Stats
noClaudeCode.intro: Claude Stats reads Claude Code's local session files to show you how many tokens you used, what it costs, and where the time is going. Right now it can't find any Claude Code data on this machine, so the dashboard is empty.

steps.heading: Install Claude Code
steps.body: Install Anthropic's Claude Code CLI from the official Anthropic documentation, then sign in once so it can write session files to your home directory.

steps.heading: Start a conversation
steps.body: Open a terminal in any project and run `claude`. Send at least one message. Claude Code writes a JSONL session log as soon as the first response arrives.

steps.heading: Come back here
steps.body: The extension watches for new session files in the background. Once the first one exists, it is picked up within a few seconds — you don't need to restart VS Code.

noClaudeCode.whatNext: Until a session exists, the status bar shows the idle icon and the dashboard stays on this welcome screen. Click "Refresh now" once you've sent a message to Claude Code.

noSessions.title: No Claude Code sessions yet
noSessions.intro: Claude Code is installed on this machine, but no sessions have been recorded yet (or the collector hasn't finished its first pass). The dashboard will populate as soon as a session exists.

steps.heading: Start or continue a conversation
steps.body: Open a terminal and run `claude` in any project folder. Send a message. Claude Code writes a JSONL log file per session into the projects directory shown below.

steps.heading: Let the collector catch up
steps.body: The extension watches ~/.claude/projects/ for changes and runs an incremental collection every few seconds (debounced). First-time collection over many historical sessions can take 10-30 seconds.

steps.heading: Refresh the dashboard
steps.body: Use the button below (or click the Claude Stats item in the status bar) to re-check. Once sessions are collected, this screen is replaced by the full dashboard automatically.

noSessions.whatNext: If you've already been using Claude Code and still see this screen after a minute, something is preventing the collector from reading the session files. Check that the paths below exist and are readable, then reload the window (Command Palette → "Developer: Reload Window").

welcome.privacyNote: Claude Stats never leaves your machine. No tokens or credentials are transmitted — everything is read locally from Claude Code's JSONL logs and aggregated into a SQLite database in your home directory.
